guides.title: Runtime enforcement
guides.summary: Runtime enforcement turns policy from advice into executable constraints by controlling which actions, data and side effects can actually pass through the system, even when the model proposes something unsafe.
guides.mentalModel: Prompting influences model behavior; runtime enforcement constrains system behavior. Gates, scoped credentials, validators, schemas, approval checks and deny rules are outside-model mechanisms that can make prohibited actions impossible or observable.
guides.whyItMatters: Models are probabilistic and context-sensitive, so a strong prompt can reduce but not eliminate unsafe proposals. For permissions, money, privacy and irreversible actions, relying on persuasion creates a single fragile layer. Runtime enforcement gives the application deterministic leverage and produces evidence that a policy was actually applied.

sections.title: Place hard constraints where side effects cross the runtime
sections.body: Identify consequential capability boundaries and enforce them before execution: validate structured inputs, check user/task authorization, scope credentials, require approvals and reject disallowed combinations. Keep model recommendations visible for diagnosis, but make the runtime independently decide whether the proposed action can execute.

sections.title: Example: prompt says 'never export customer data'
sections.body: An agent is prompted never to export full customer records, yet an injected document persuades it to call an export tool. If the runtime exposes broad credentials, the prompt failure becomes a breach. With scoped capabilities and a deny rule for external exports, the proposed call is blocked and recorded regardless of the model's text.

failureModes: Using prompt refusal language as the only protection for sensitive tools.
Putting runtime gates after a side effect has already occurred.
Creating enforcement rules without observable reason codes or audit evidence.
heuristics: Enforce consequential policy before side effects execute.
Scope credentials and capabilities to the current task.
Return structured block reasons so failures remain diagnosable.
takeaways: Runtime enforcement constrains actions, not just model intentions.
Hard guarantees require controls outside the model.
Blocked actions should produce evidence, not disappear silently.

guides.title: SHIP / BLOCK / INCONCLUSIVE
guides.summary: Release evaluation should end in an explicit decision state: SHIP when evidence clears required gates, BLOCK when a veto or unacceptable regression is present, and INCONCLUSIVE when evidence is too weak to decide safely.
guides.mentalModel: These three states separate product quality from evidence quality. BLOCK means evidence is strong enough to show a problem; INCONCLUSIVE means the system has not earned either confidence to ship or proof to reject.
guides.whyItMatters: Teams often force every evaluation into pass/fail, which encourages shipping on noisy wins or blocking on weak signals. An inconclusive state creates room to collect more data. Explicit vetoes also prevent strong aggregate scores from averaging away safety, cost or slice regressions that should stop release.

sections.title: Synthesize evidence through gates and sufficiency checks
sections.body: Define required quality floors, critical vetoes and evidence-sufficiency criteria before evaluation runs. First apply non-negotiable vetoes, then check whether observed improvements or regressions are large enough relative to uncertainty, and only then decide SHIP or BLOCK. If evidence width, sample size or judge reliability cannot support the conclusion, return INCONCLUSIVE and specify what evidence is missing.

sections.title: Example: average score rises while safety slice collapses
sections.body: A model update improves the aggregate score by four points, but a safety-critical refund slice drops below its release floor. The correct outcome is BLOCK, not SHIP with a warning. In another run, the aggregate gain is one point with a very small sample; no veto fires, but evidence is too weak, so the outcome is INCONCLUSIVE.

failureModes: Reducing every evaluation to one aggregate pass threshold.
Treating no detected regression as proof that shipping is safe.
Using INCONCLUSIVE as a vague escape instead of naming the missing evidence.
heuristics: Define vetoes before seeing candidate results.
Separate evidence sufficiency from candidate quality.
Make every INCONCLUSIVE decision name the next evidence needed.
takeaways: SHIP, BLOCK and INCONCLUSIVE are evidence states, not sentiment labels.
Critical vetoes should not be averaged away.
Insufficient evidence is a legitimate result that should drive the next experiment.

guides.title: Adapter fine-tuning
guides.summary: Adapter fine-tuning changes a small trainable component while keeping most base-model weights fixed, making targeted behavior adaptation cheaper and easier to version than full fine-tuning when a measured task gap justifies training.
guides.mentalModel: Adapters separate base capability from task-specific parameter changes. Methods such as LoRA express an update through a compact set of trainable parameters; serving can load or route adapters without maintaining a completely separate full model for every variant.
guides.whyItMatters: Fine-tuning is often proposed before teams prove that prompt, context or retrieval changes are insufficient. Adapter methods reduce training and storage cost, but they still add data, evaluation, versioning and serving complexity. The right question is not whether adapters are efficient, but whether they close a stable measured gap better than simpler alternatives.

sections.title: Train only after a strong baseline exposes a persistent gap
sections.body: Build and evaluate a prompt/RAG baseline, define the behavior that remains wrong, curate training data that represents that gap and keep held-out evaluation separate. Compare adapter, quantized-adapter and full-fine-tune options on task quality, training cost, serving complexity and rollback. Version the adapter with its base-model dependency and evaluation evidence.

sections.title: Example: style classification remains inconsistent
sections.body: A domain classifier improves with prompt examples and retrieval but still misses a stable set of labels. The team curates representative corrections, holds out a failure set and trains a LoRA adapter. The adapter ships only if it closes the measured gap without creating unacceptable serving or regression cost; otherwise the simpler baseline remains.

failureModes: Fine-tuning before measuring a strong non-training baseline.
Training adapters on raw production logs without curation or held-out evaluation.
Ignoring base-model compatibility and serving lifecycle when versioning adapters.
heuristics: Require a persistent measured behavior gap before training.
Keep training data and held-out evaluation evidence separate.
Version adapter, base model and serving policy as one operational unit.
takeaways: Adapters reduce parameter cost, not the need for evaluation.
Fine-tuning should answer a measured gap, not a preference for training.
Serving and rollback complexity belong in the adaptation decision.

guides.title: Curriculum decomposition
guides.summary: Curriculum decomposition turns learning objectives into an ordered set of teachable decisions, concepts and practices, preserving prerequisites and transfer instead of generating a pile of loosely related lessons.
guides.mentalModel: A curriculum is a dependency-aware learning path. Decomposition asks what the learner must understand first, what decision each unit enables, what practice proves the transition and what can be deferred without breaking later learning.
guides.whyItMatters: AI makes lesson production cheap, so curriculum quality increasingly depends on sequencing and omission. If every interesting topic becomes a unit, learners receive breadth without a usable mental model. Decomposition keeps the course aligned to outcomes and makes content generation subordinate to a coherent learning progression.

sections.title: Decompose backward from outcome and prerequisite
sections.body: Start with the final learner decision or artifact, identify the concepts required to produce it, then arrange them by dependency rather than by source-material order. Give each unit one clear transition: what becomes possible after this unit that was not possible before? Attach practice where the transition needs evidence, and merge or defer topics that do not create a distinct learning step.

sections.title: Example: an RAG course mirrors a documentation table of contents
sections.body: A course copies docs into chapters on embeddings, vector databases, chunking, reranking and evaluation. Learners know terms but cannot diagnose a failed pipeline. Re-decomposition starts from the task 'identify why evidence was missed or noisy', then orders retrieval units, ranking, authority and evaluation around that decision with a failure lab as evidence.

failureModes: Using source-document order as curriculum order.
Creating one lesson per topic even when several do not represent distinct learner transitions.
Adding practice activities that are engaging but do not prove the stated objective.
heuristics: Sequence by prerequisite and learner decision, not author convenience.
Give each unit a distinct observable learning transition.
Merge or defer material that does not change what the learner can do.
takeaways: Curriculum is an ordered dependency system, not a content inventory.
Cheap generation makes omission and sequencing more important.
A good unit earns its place by enabling a distinct learner transition.

guides.title: Automation maintenance
guides.summary: Automation creates leverage only when its monitoring, exceptions, dependency drift and repair cost stay lower than the work it removes; maintenance is part of automation ROI, not an afterthought.
guides.mentalModel: Every automation creates a new operational surface: triggers can drift, APIs change, credentials expire, edge cases accumulate and users discover paths the original workflow did not model. Net leverage equals saved repetitive work minus maintenance and exception handling.
guides.whyItMatters: Solo operators are especially vulnerable to maintenance traps because every failed automation returns to the same person who built it. Automating too broadly can replace ten minutes of daily manual work with hours of weekly debugging. Designing upkeep explicitly keeps automation bounded to repeatable, observable and recoverable work.

sections.title: Budget maintenance before automating
sections.body: For each workflow, record dependency count, expected exception rate, observability, ownership and recovery path. Automate the stable reversible core first, keep exception queues visible, and define who or what notices silent failure. Review maintenance hours and failure causes regularly; retire or simplify automations whose upkeep exceeds the value they create.

sections.title: Example: content pipeline saves ten minutes but breaks every week
sections.body: A solo founder automates a publishing pipeline across four SaaS tools. It saves ten minutes per post but fails weekly because tokens expire and schemas change. A simpler workflow keeps drafting automated but makes publication an explicit review step, cutting dependency count and reducing maintenance enough to create real leverage.

failureModes: Measuring automation success only by manual steps removed.
Automating exception-heavy work before the exception taxonomy is understood.
Leaving silent failure detection and credential renewal to memory.
heuristics: Include maintenance hours and exception handling in ROI.
Automate stable reversible work before high-variance consequential work.
Retire automation that consistently costs more to maintain than it saves.
takeaways: Automation creates an operational surface as well as leverage.
Maintenance cost belongs in the original design decision.
The best automation is often bounded rather than maximal.
